C) Thor Heyerdahl first crossed the Pacific on a raft in 1947.
D) Seabirds feed plastic fragments to their chicks, leading to malnutrition and death.
D
C
B
A
Medium
Evaluating Relevance
Supporting Evidence & Details

The argument is about plastic pollution threatening marine life. A, B, and D all contribute to this argument. C is about Heyerdahl's raft journey — a notable historical event but entirely unrelated to the plastic pollution and marine life argument.

A researcher wants to determine whether a new reading curriculum improves reading comprehension in third-grade students. The researcher has pre- and post-test reading comprehension scores for a class that used the new curriculum.

What is the most critical limitation of this study?
A) The study doesn't measure reading speed in addition to comprehension
B) Without a control group of students using a different curriculum, improvement could be due to normal development or other factors unrelated to the new curriculum
C) The study only covers third grade students and may not apply to other grade levels
D) The tests used to measure comprehension may not be standardized
B
A
D
C
Medium
Completing Research
Supporting Evidence & Details

Without a control group, you can't attribute the improvement to the curriculum — students improve in reading naturally over a year regardless of curriculum. B identifies this critical flaw. A is about reading speed (minor). C is about generalizability (secondary concern). D is about test quality (important but secondary).

Which detail is LEAST relevant to the central argument?

Passage: 'The decline in bee populations poses a critical threat to global food security, since bees are responsible for pollinating approximately one-third of the food crops consumed by humans. Colony collapse disorder, pesticide exposure, habitat loss, and parasitic mites have all been identified as contributing factors. Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, in Physics and Chemistry. Restoring wildflower meadows and reducing pesticide use in agricultural areas are key strategies for reversing pollinator decline.'

A) Bees pollinate approximately one-third of human food crops.
B) Colony collapse disorder and pesticide exposure contribute to bee decline.
C) Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
D) Restoring wildflower meadows is a key strategy for reversing pollinator decline.
A
C
B
D
Medium
Evaluating Relevance
Supporting Evidence & Details

The argument is about bee population decline and food security threats. A, B, and D are all directly relevant. C is about Marie Curie's Nobel Prizes — completely unrelated to bees, pollination, or food security.

A student claims: 'Practicing a musical instrument during childhood leads to stronger executive function skills in adulthood.' The student has data showing that adults who played instruments as children score higher on executive function tests.

Which concern most undermines the student's claim?
A) The data doesn't specify which instruments participants played
B) Families with resources for music lessons may also provide other cognitive enrichment, and children with stronger executive function may be more likely to stick with music — making the causal direction unclear
C) The study doesn't include data from participants who began playing instruments as adults
D) The executive function tests used may favor certain types of cognitive skills
C
B
A
D
Medium
Completing Research
Supporting Evidence & Details

This identifies REVERSE CAUSATION and CONFOUNDING: (1) children with stronger executive function might be MORE LIKELY to stick with music; (2) wealthier families provide both music lessons AND other enrichment. Both problems make it unclear whether music CAUSED better executive function. B identifies both concerns. A, C, D are minor.

Which detail is LEAST relevant to the following argument?

Passage: 'Solitary confinement in prisons is associated with severe psychological harm, including depression, anxiety, hallucinations, and self-harm. Inmates held in isolation lack meaningful human contact for 22 or more hours per day. The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners define prolonged solitary confinement (more than 15 days) as torture. Nelson Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island from 1964 to 1982. These psychological effects persist after release, complicating reintegration into society.'

A) Inmates in isolation lack meaningful human contact for 22 or more hours per day.
B) The UN defines prolonged solitary confinement as torture.
C) Nelson Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island from 1964 to 1982.
D) Psychological effects of solitary confinement persist after release.
C
B
A
D
Medium
Evaluating Relevance
Supporting Evidence & Details

The argument is about psychological harm from solitary confinement. A, B, and D are all directly relevant. C is about Mandela's imprisonment — while contextually related to prison, his specific imprisonment does not logically contribute to the argument about solitary confinement's psychological effects.

A researcher argues: 'Increased police presence in high-crime neighborhoods deters criminal activity.' The researcher has data showing a correlation between police patrol hours and crime rates across a city.
Which concern most undermines the ability to draw a causal conclusion from this data?
A) The data doesn't distinguish between types of crime
B) Police may be deployed to high-crime areas precisely because crime is already high there, making it unclear whether police presence reduces crime or crime levels determine police deployment
C) The study doesn't account for seasonal variation in crime rates
D) The correlation doesn't specify how many officers constitute increased presence
B
C
A
D
Medium
Completing Research
Supporting Evidence & Details

This is a classic REVERSE CAUSATION problem: police are sent WHERE crime is high, so correlation between police presence and crime doesn't tell you if more police → less crime or if more crime → more police. B identifies this fundamental flaw. A is minor. C is a secondary concern. D is about definition.

Which detail is LEAST relevant to the following argument?

Passage: 'The rapid urbanization of coastal cities in Asia increases vulnerability to flooding from sea level rise and more intense tropical storms. Impervious surfaces in cities prevent rainwater from absorbing into the ground, increasing runoff and flood risk. The poet Li Bai, considered one of the greatest poets of the Tang Dynasty, wrote extensively about rivers and water. Degradation of mangroves and wetlands that once buffered coastlines has further amplified storm surge damage.'

A) Impervious surfaces increase runoff and flood risk.
B) The poet Li Bai wrote extensively about rivers and water.
C) Degradation of mangroves has amplified storm surge damage.
D) Rapid urbanization of coastal cities increases vulnerability to flooding.
B
D
C
A
Medium
Evaluating Relevance
Supporting Evidence & Details

The argument is about coastal flooding vulnerability from urbanization. A, C, and D are directly relevant. B is about the Tang Dynasty poet Li Bai — while poetically connected to water themes, this detail has no logical role in an argument about urban flooding and climate vulnerability.

A student argues: 'High sugar consumption causes aggressive behavior in children.' The student has found a correlation between sugar consumption at birthday parties and subsequent aggressive behavior.

What is the most critical flaw in this reasoning?
A) The study doesn't control for the type of sugar consumed
B) Birthday parties involve excitement, social competition, and reduced adult supervision — factors that could cause both higher sugar consumption AND aggressive behavior, making sugar consumption a spurious correlation
C) The study doesn't measure aggression before the party
D) The aggressive behavior was measured only immediately after the party
C
D
B
A
Medium
Completing Research
Supporting Evidence & Details

This is a classic CONFOUNDING VARIABLE problem. Birthday parties create excitement and social competition INDEPENDENTLY — these factors could cause aggression regardless of sugar. Sugar consumption is correlated with aggression at parties, but both are caused by the party environment. B identifies this confounding factor. A, C, D are minor methodological concerns.

Which detail is LEAST relevant to the central argument?

Passage: 'Rising tuition costs at American universities have made higher education increasingly inaccessible to students from low-income families. Between 1980 and 2020, inflation-adjusted tuition at four-year universities rose by over 300%. Student loan debt in the United States now exceeds $1.7 trillion, burdening graduates for decades. Harvard University was founded in 1636, making it the oldest institution of higher education in the United States. Policy proposals to address the crisis include debt cancellation, tuition-free community college, and expansion of grant aid.'

A) Inflation-adjusted tuition rose by over 300% between 1980 and 2020.
B) Harvard University was founded in 1636.
C) Student loan debt exceeds $1.7 trillion.
D) Policy proposals include debt cancellation and tuition-free community college.
C
B
D
A
Medium
Evaluating Relevance
Supporting Evidence & Details

The argument is about rising tuition costs, student debt, and policy solutions. A, C, and D are all directly relevant. B is about Harvard's 1636 founding — historically notable but logically irrelevant to the argument about tuition costs and accessibility.

Passage: 'A survey of 500 adults found that those who read fiction regularly scored significantly higher on measures of empathy than those who read primarily non-fiction or did not read for pleasure. The researchers noted, however, that highly empathetic people may simply be more drawn to fiction in the first place.'

Based on the passage, it can most reasonably be inferred that
Non-fiction readers lack the capacity for empathetic thinking
The researchers are confident that reading fiction increases empathy
Reading fiction causes higher empathy in all readers
The relationship between fiction reading and empathy may reflect reader selection rather than a causal effect of reading
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The researchers' note about 'highly empathetic people may be more drawn to fiction' is precisely a REVERSE CAUSATION concern — the empathy may precede the fiction reading, not result from it. C accurately captures this inference. A over-infers (causal claim not established). B is contradicted by the caveat. D is extreme and unsupported.

Passage: 'The giant squid was known for centuries only from carcasses and fragments recovered from the stomachs of sperm whales. It was not until 2004 that researchers first photographed a live giant squid in its natural habitat, at a depth of approximately 900 meters.'

It can be inferred from the passage that before 2004,
Scientists had no evidence that giant squids existed
Sperm whales were the primary predators of giant squids
Giant squids did not exist in their natural habitat and lived only near the surface
Observing a living giant squid in its natural environment was extraordinarily difficult
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The fact that no live photo was taken until 2004 despite centuries of knowledge suggests the extreme DIFFICULTY of observing them alive in their deep-water habitat. C is the most supported inference. A is contradicted (they had carcasses as evidence). B is contradicted (they had carcass/fragment evidence for centuries). D may be true but the passage doesn't imply sperm whales are the PRIMARY predator.

Passage: 'Countries that have legalized and regulated cannabis markets have seen declines in cannabis purchases from illegal dealers in those regions. However, cross-border trafficking to neighboring areas where cannabis remains illegal has increased significantly in some cases.'

The passage most strongly suggests that
Cannabis legalization is ineffective as a policy because illegal activity increases
Cannabis legalization reduces domestic illegal sales but may shift rather than eliminate some illegal trafficking
Legalizing cannabis eliminates all illegal drug trade activity
The effects of cannabis legalization on illegal markets vary depending on whether neighboring jurisdictions have also legalized
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: legal markets → fewer local illegal sales BUT MORE cross-border trafficking where it's illegal elsewhere. D accurately captures both effects: reduces domestic illegal sales but shifts (not eliminates) trafficking. A is an over-inference. B mischaracterizes (legal markets DO reduce local illegal sales). C is about what would happen with neighboring legalization — not directly stated.

Passage: 'Despite being separated by thousands of miles, the pyramids of ancient Egypt and the stepped pyramids of Mesoamerica were built independently, centuries apart. While some authors have proposed extra-terrestrial or lost civilization explanations for this similarity, archaeologists attribute the parallel development to the practical and symbolic advantages of the pyramid form — a shape that is structurally stable, visible from a distance, and naturally suggests elevation toward the divine.'

The passage implies that the archaeological consensus is that
Similar architectural forms can arise independently when different cultures face similar practical and symbolic needs
Ancient Egyptian and Mesoamerican civilizations were in contact with each other
Pyramid shapes were uniquely suited to their climatic conditions
Extra-terrestrial influences on ancient architecture cannot be completely ruled out
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The archaeologists attribute the similarity to PRACTICAL AND SYMBOLIC ADVANTAGES of the form — implying that different cultures independently discovered the same solution to the same needs. C captures this 'convergent development' implication. A is directly contradicted ('independently'). B is not mentioned (climate). D contradicts the passage — archaeologists DON'T use extra-terrestrial explanations.

Passage: 'The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone in 1995 produced cascading ecological effects. Elk populations declined and changed their grazing behavior, which allowed riverbank vegetation to recover. The returning vegetation stabilized banks, changed river flow patterns, and attracted beavers, whose dams created wetland habitats. Songbird and fish populations subsequently increased.'

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
Wolves directly improved water quality in Yellowstone's rivers
Beaver populations were zero in Yellowstone before wolf reintroduction
The removal of wolves had previously triggered a chain of ecological changes throughout the park
Elk are the primary threat to ecological balance in all natural parks
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

Since the REINTRODUCTION of wolves triggered positive cascading changes (elk behavior changed, vegetation recovered, rivers changed, beavers returned), it can be inferred that the REMOVAL of wolves had previously triggered the REVERSE chain — elk overgrazed, banks eroded, rivers changed, etc. B captures this logical reversal. A is not supported (water quality not mentioned). C is too broad. D is an over-inference (beavers may have been reduced, not necessarily zero).

Passage: 'Antibiotic resistance has emerged as a major threat to global health, with drug-resistant infections killing an estimated 700,000 people annually. Much of this resistance has developed because antibiotics have been prescribed for viral infections — against which they are entirely ineffective — or because patients fail to complete their full course of treatment.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Completing a full course of antibiotics guarantees that resistance will not develop
Viruses will eventually become resistant to antibiotics as well
All antibiotic prescriptions are unnecessary and should be eliminated
Reducing inappropriate antibiotic use could help slow the development of resistance
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage identifies two causes of resistance: prescribing for viruses AND incomplete courses. It follows logically that reducing these practices could slow resistance development. B directly follows. A is extreme (passage doesn't say all prescriptions are inappropriate). C is a biological misunderstanding (viruses can't develop antibiotic resistance). D over-infers (completion helps but doesn't guarantee resistance prevention).

Passage: 'Observations of chimpanzee groups in the wild have documented tool use, strategic deception, cultural transmission of behaviors across generations, and even rudimentary forms of political coalition-building. These findings have required researchers to revise earlier assumptions about what distinguishes human cognition from that of other primates.'

From the passage, it can be inferred that researchers previously believed
Observations of wild primates were not scientifically valid before these studies
Chimpanzees were incapable of any form of intelligent behavior
Chimpanzees and humans share a common ancestor but diverged significantly in cognitive ability
The behaviors observed in chimpanzees — tool use, deception, culture, and political behavior — were thought to be exclusively human
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage says the findings 'required researchers to REVISE EARLIER ASSUMPTIONS about what distinguishes human cognition' — implying the earlier assumption was that these specific behaviors (tool use, deception, culture, coalition-building) DISTINGUISHED humans and were thought to be uniquely human. B captures this. A is too extreme (they didn't think chimps had NO intelligence). C is about ancestry (not mentioned). D is unsupported.

Passage: 'Rent control policies, which cap the amount landlords can charge for existing rentals, are intended to protect long-term residents from displacement. Economists note, however, that landlords in rent-controlled areas often convert rental units to condominiums or allow properties to deteriorate rather than maintain them, and that new construction in rent-controlled cities tends to decline.'

Based on the passage, it can be inferred that
Rent control successfully protects all low-income residents from displacement
Economists universally oppose rent control policies
Rent control may achieve some short-term goals while producing unintended consequences that affect housing supply
Rent control is always economically harmful and should be abolished
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows rent control's INTENT (protect residents) vs. economists' noted UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES (conversion, deterioration, less construction). C captures this tension accurately. A ignores the unintended consequences. B is too extreme ('always harmful,' 'should be abolished' — the passage doesn't advocate a policy position). D is too strong — the passage cites economists noting consequences, not universal opposition.

Passage: 'Studies of children who were adopted internationally before age two and raised in high-resource environments consistently show that early nutritional deprivation — even if corrected within the first few years of life — produces lasting differences in cognitive test scores compared to non-deprived comparison groups. The differences are smaller when adoption occurs in the first year.'

It can be most reasonably inferred that
High-resource adoptive environments fully eliminate the effects of early deprivation
Children adopted before age one are cognitively indistinguishable from non-deprived children
There appear to be sensitive periods in early development during which nutritional deprivation has disproportionate long-term cognitive effects
Nutritional deprivation after age two has no effect on cognitive development
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: early deprivation → lasting cognitive differences EVEN AFTER correction, AND smaller differences when adoption (correction) occurs in the first year. This pattern implies SENSITIVE PERIODS — earlier intervention matters more, implying some periods are more critical than others. C captures this inference. A is not supported (the passage only covers early deprivation). B is too strong ('indistinguishable' — passage says 'smaller differences,' not zero). D is directly contradicted by 'lasting differences.'

Passage: 'The average surface temperature of Earth has increased by approximately 1.1°C since pre-industrial times. Climate scientists project that without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, temperatures will rise by 1.5-4.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, depending on emission scenarios. At higher warming levels, risks of extreme weather events, sea level rise, and ecosystem disruption increase substantially.'

Based on the passage, it can most reasonably be inferred that
Exceeding 1.5°C of warming will cause immediate catastrophic collapse of global ecosystems
The range of projected warming reflects scientific uncertainty about future emission levels and climate sensitivity
Climate scientists believe warming above 4.5°C is impossible under any scenario
Greenhouse gas emissions are currently declining globally as a result of climate policy
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The 1.5-4.5°C range 'depending on emission scenarios' directly implies the range reflects uncertainty about BOTH what emissions will be AND how the climate will respond. B captures this inference precisely. A is too extreme ('immediate catastrophic collapse' is not stated). C is the opposite of what would explain the need for 'significant reductions.' D is a misreading — the range IS the projection, not an upper limit.

Passage: 'When archaeologists excavated a 5,000-year-old cemetery in what is now Denmark, they found that the individuals buried with the most elaborate grave goods — weapons, jewelry, and tools — had significantly higher levels of dental enamel defects associated with childhood nutritional stress than those buried more simply. The researchers suggested this pattern may reflect upward social mobility.'

The researchers' explanation implies that
Wealth in ancient Denmark was entirely inherited and could not be acquired through merit
Individuals who achieved high status in this society did not necessarily begin life in privileged circumstances
Dental enamel defects were caused by the stress of achieving social status
The elaborate grave goods were placed by the deceased before their deaths
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

If the HIGH-STATUS individuals (elaborate grave goods) showed MORE childhood nutritional stress, they likely came from POORER backgrounds originally and achieved high status later — implying STATUS was not simply inherited. B captures this 'upward mobility' implication precisely. A is the opposite of what the data suggests. C misattributes cause (enamel defects from childhood nutrition, not 'stress of achieving status'). D is illogical.

Passage: 'Deep-sea fishing vessels using trawl nets drag weighted nets across the ocean floor, capturing target species but also destroying fragile benthic habitats and catching large quantities of non-target species — a problem known as bycatch. Bycatch can amount to 40% or more of total catch in some fisheries.'

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
The ecological impact of trawl fishing extends beyond the target species being harvested
All deep-sea fishing should be prohibited to protect ocean ecosystems
At least 40% of all fish caught globally are released back into the ocean
Trawl fishing is less efficient than surface fishing methods
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage describes habitat destruction AND non-target species capture — both effects beyond the target species. C accurately captures this: the impact extends beyond target species. A is an extreme policy recommendation not implied. B about efficiency is not discussed. D misreads '40% bycatch in SOME FISHERIES' as a global statistic.

Passage: 'The playwright Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot premiered in Paris in 1953 to bewildered audiences and mixed reviews. Within a decade, it had become one of the most performed and analyzed plays of the twentieth century, widely regarded as a masterwork of existentialist drama.'

From the passage, it can be inferred that
The initial reception of a work is not necessarily a reliable guide to its long-term cultural significance
Parisian theater audiences in the 1950s were generally unsophisticated
Existentialist drama was not popular in France until after Godot's success
Beckett deliberately confused his audience as an artistic strategy
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The contrast between 'bewildered audiences, mixed reviews' in 1953 and 'masterwork' status within a decade directly implies that initial reception was a poor predictor of long-term significance. B is the clear inference. A is speculative (the passage doesn't describe Beckett's intentions). C is too broad a generalization. D is not supported by the passage.

Passage: 'Economists studying the effects of the minimum wage have found mixed results. Some studies show that moderate increases in the minimum wage do not significantly reduce employment, while others find small employment declines in affected industries. The variation in findings appears related to local labor market conditions, the magnitude of the wage increase, and the time horizon studied.'

The passage most strongly suggests that
Minimum wage increases are economically beneficial in all circumstances
Economists have failed to conduct rigorous research on minimum wage effects
Minimum wage increases always reduce employment
The economic effects of minimum wage increases depend on contextual factors and cannot be summarized by a single universal finding
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage explicitly shows MIXED RESULTS that vary by 'local labor market conditions, magnitude of increase, and time horizon' — directly implying that context matters and there is no universal answer. B captures this. A and D are contradicted by 'mixed results.' C is unsupported — the passage describes existing research without criticizing its rigor.

Passage: 'The bones of early whales found in Pakistan and India show a progressive series of adaptations over millions of years: from fully terrestrial ancestors with full limbs, to semi-aquatic forms with reduced hind limbs, to forms with vestigial hind limbs and elongated bodies suited to swimming, to fully aquatic descendants without functional hind limbs.'

From the passage, it can be most reasonably inferred that
Early whale ancestors were aquatic organisms that temporarily adapted to land
Whales are more closely related to fish than to land-dwelling mammals
The fossil record provides evidence for a gradual evolutionary transition in the whale lineage from land to water
Whales lost their hind limbs in a single rapid evolutionary event
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage describes a 'progressive series of adaptations over millions of years' moving from terrestrial to aquatic forms — the definition of gradual evolutionary transition. B is the direct inference. A is contradicted by 'over millions of years.' C reverses the direction (land → water, not water → land → water). D is not supported (the passage implies land ancestry).

Passage: 'Research on implicit bias — unconscious associations that affect judgment — finds that people who score high on measures of implicit racial bias often sincerely believe they are unbiased and may actively hold anti-racist beliefs. Training programs designed to reduce implicit bias have shown limited effectiveness in changing actual behavior in most studies.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Sincerely held anti-racist beliefs eliminate the influence of implicit bias on behavior
Implicit bias tests do not accurately measure racial attitudes
Implicit bias cannot be reduced under any circumstances
Addressing implicit bias in behavior is more complex than simply increasing awareness or changing conscious attitudes
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: (1) people can be implicitly biased while sincerely believing otherwise, and (2) bias training has limited effectiveness on behavior. Together these imply that awareness and conscious attitude change are NOT sufficient to change behavior — the problem is more complex. C captures this complexity. A is too extreme (training has LIMITED effectiveness, not NO possibility). B is directly contradicted. D is not discussed.

Passage: 'Despite extensive lobbying by pharmaceutical companies, several European countries have implemented reference pricing systems, in which the government pays for drugs based on the prices charged in other comparable countries. Countries using these systems have achieved significantly lower pharmaceutical prices than countries without them.'

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
All countries will eventually adopt reference pricing systems
Reference pricing systems have no effect on pharmaceutical innovation
Pharmaceutical companies support reference pricing because it ensures fair international prices
The lobbying by pharmaceutical companies against reference pricing suggests these systems reduce company revenues
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The pharmaceutical companies LOBBIED AGAINST reference pricing — and reference pricing leads to LOWER prices. Logically, companies lobby against things that reduce their revenues. B captures this inference. A is contradicted (they lobbied AGAINST it, not for it). C is speculative. D is not discussed in the passage.

Passage: 'The decline of traditional apprenticeship systems in manufacturing sectors has coincided with growing employer complaints about skill gaps in the technical workforce. Countries that have maintained robust apprenticeship systems, such as Germany, report significantly lower rates of youth unemployment.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Youth unemployment in countries with apprenticeship systems is essentially zero
The decline of apprenticeship systems may have contributed to both skill gaps and youth unemployment in affected countries
Germany's economic success is due primarily to its apprenticeship system
Apprenticeship systems are the only effective method for technical skills training
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage presents two correlations: (1) apprenticeship decline → skill gaps + employer complaints; (2) maintained apprenticeships → lower youth unemployment. The logical implication is that apprenticeship decline contributed to these problems. B captures this. A is too strong ('only effective method'). C oversimplifies Germany's success. D over-infers 'significantly lower' as 'essentially zero.'

Passage: 'For most of human evolutionary history, access to high-calorie, sweet, and fatty foods was limited and unpredictable. The human preference for such foods — which persists in contemporary populations — appears to have been adaptive in environments of food scarcity. In modern food environments with abundant, inexpensive calorie-dense foods, this preference contributes to overconsumption and obesity.'

From the passage, it can be most reasonably inferred that
Modern humans should eliminate all preference for sweet and fatty foods
Human food preferences evolved to suit modern food environments
A trait that was adaptive in ancestral environments may become maladaptive in a radically changed environment
Obesity is entirely caused by evolutionary food preferences
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage describes a trait (preference for high-calorie foods) that was ADAPTIVE then but now CONTRIBUTES TO OBESITY in a changed environment. This is precisely the evolutionary concept of mismatch — an adaptation becoming maladaptive in a new context. C captures this inference. A is backwards. B says 'entirely caused' which is too strong. D is a recommendation not implied.

Passage: 'In the 1840s, physician Ignaz Semmelweis discovered that requiring doctors to wash their hands with chlorinated lime solution before delivering babies dramatically reduced maternal mortality rates in his ward from approximately 10% to below 2%. His findings were largely rejected by the medical establishment of the time, and Semmelweis died in an asylum in 1865, years before germ theory provided the scientific explanation for why handwashing worked.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Hand washing is the most important medical intervention ever discovered
The medical establishment in the 1840s was deliberately corrupt and opposed to patient welfare
Semmelweis was correct about the importance of handwashing but was unable to provide an acceptable theoretical explanation for his findings
Germ theory was already widely understood in Semmelweis's time but suppressed by hospital administrators
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: Semmelweis's EMPIRICAL FINDING worked (10% → below 2%) BUT was rejected, and the theoretical explanation (germ theory) came later. The implication is that without a theoretical framework, empirically correct findings can be rejected — his data was right, but he lacked the explanatory mechanism. A captures this precisely. B is too extreme. C directly contradicts ('years before germ theory'). D is an unsupported superlative.

Passage: 'Teenagers who participate in team sports show higher rates of college attendance and lower rates of depression in adulthood than non-participating peers. However, researchers caution that teenagers from more affluent families are both more likely to participate in organized sports and more likely to attend college and have better mental health outcomes due to resources unrelated to sports.'

Based on the passage, it can be inferred that
Participating in team sports guarantees better adult outcomes for all teenagers
Researchers have definitively concluded that sports do not affect mental health
Sports participation is beneficial only for teenagers from low-income families
The positive outcomes associated with sports participation may reflect pre-existing socioeconomic advantages rather than a direct effect of sports
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The researchers' caveat about affluent families describes a CONFOUND: affluence → both sports participation AND better outcomes — making it unclear if sports CAUSE the better outcomes. B accurately captures this inference about confounding. A is an over-inference. C is the opposite of what the confound describes. D is too strong — researchers caution about interpretation, not conclude no effect.

Passage: 'Modern wheat varieties developed during the Green Revolution of the 1960s produce dramatically higher yields than traditional varieties. However, these high-yield varieties require substantial inputs of synthetic fertilizers and irrigation to achieve their potential. In regions where these inputs are unavailable, traditional low-yield but drought-resistant varieties often outperform the modern alternatives.'

It can be most reasonably inferred from the passage that
Agricultural innovation must be evaluated in context, since solutions effective in resource-rich settings may be less effective or even inferior in resource-constrained environments
The adoption of Green Revolution wheat varieties is appropriate only for wealthy nations with advanced agricultural infrastructure
Traditional agricultural practices are always preferable to modern alternatives
Modern high-yield wheat varieties are superior to traditional varieties in all agricultural contexts
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: modern varieties → higher yields WITH inputs, BUT traditional varieties OUTPERFORM in low-input regions. This implies context-dependence — the 'best' variety depends on available resources. C captures this contextual lesson. A is contradicted (traditional varieties outperform in low-input contexts). B is too restrictive about wealthy nations. D is the opposite extreme.

Passage: 'A linguist studying a remote indigenous language documented approximately 40 native speakers, all elderly. Younger community members, who had grown up in a region where the national language dominated education, media, and employment, used the indigenous language rarely and with limited fluency.'

From the passage, it can most reasonably be inferred that
The linguist's documentation project will be sufficient to preserve the language for future generations
Young community members have deliberately chosen to abandon their indigenous language
The national language is superior to the indigenous language for communication purposes
The indigenous language will likely become extinct within a few generations unless active revitalization efforts succeed
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

With only ~40 elderly speakers and young people having limited fluency, the language has no natural transmission pathway to the next generation — the typical pattern of language extinction. A is the most supported inference. B is a value judgment not supported by the passage. C is contradicted by the implication of extinction risk — documentation preserves knowledge of the language, not the living language. D implies deliberate choice; the passage suggests structural reasons (education, media, employment).

Passage: 'The same mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes that substantially increase an individual's risk of developing breast and ovarian cancer also appear to have been maintained in the human population at relatively stable frequencies. This has led some researchers to hypothesize that these mutations may confer benefits in some contexts — perhaps related to enhanced immune function or fertility — that offset their cancer risk.'

The passage implies that
Mutations that cause disease are always eventually eliminated from human populations
The persistence of BRCA1/2 mutations in the population is inconsistent with natural selection and requires non-evolutionary explanation
The relatively stable frequency of these mutations in the population suggests they may not be purely harmful across all contexts and life stages
All genetic mutations that increase disease risk must confer reproductive benefits to be maintained
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

If natural selection eliminates purely harmful mutations, the persistence of BRCA1/2 at stable frequencies IMPLIES they aren't purely harmful — there may be compensating benefits. C captures this inference. A is the assumption the passage CHALLENGES. B is contradicted — the researchers offer an EVOLUTIONARY (natural selection) explanation. D is too absolute ('all... must').

Passage: 'Research in cognitive psychology has established that human memory does not work like a recording device that captures and replays events accurately. Instead, memories are reconstructive — each time a memory is retrieved, it is rebuilt from partial information and can be altered by subsequent experiences, suggestions, and expectations.'

Based on the passage, it can be most reasonably inferred that
All memories are completely unreliable and should be discarded as evidence
Memory improves significantly when people are allowed to retrieve it multiple times
Cognitive psychology has proven that human memory is entirely fictional
The reconstructive nature of memory means that eyewitness testimony in legal settings may be less reliable than commonly assumed
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

If memories are reconstructive and can be altered by subsequent experiences and suggestions, then eyewitness testimony — which relies on accurate memory — may be less reliable than the assumption of a 'recording device.' B is the direct, appropriately scoped inference. A and D are too extreme ('completely unreliable,' 'entirely fictional'). C is not supported — multiple retrievals might actually ALTER memory more.

Passage: 'In ecosystems with abundant food resources, animal species often exhibit increased behavioral flexibility — using novel tools, exploiting new food sources, and adapting more quickly to environmental changes. In resource-scarce environments, the same species tend to rely more heavily on fixed, inherited behavioral routines.'

From the passage, it can be most reasonably inferred that
Environmental conditions have no effect on animal behavior
Fixed behavioral routines are always inferior to flexible responses in evolutionary terms
Behavioral flexibility may be a function of available resources as much as innate cognitive capacity
Animals in resource-abundant environments are genetically more intelligent than those in scarce environments
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows the SAME SPECIES behaves more flexibly with abundant resources and less flexibly when scarce — implying that RESOURCE AVAILABILITY (environment), not just innate capacity, influences behavioral flexibility. B captures this inference. A is not supported (same species, so genetic intelligence is controlled). C is too strong ('always inferior'). D directly contradicts the passage.

Passage: 'Several major technology companies have voluntarily published annual transparency reports disclosing government requests for user data. Critics note, however, that these reports are produced unilaterally by the companies themselves and are not independently audited or verified.'

The passage most strongly implies that
The reliability of company self-reported transparency data is limited by the absence of independent verification
Government agencies make unreasonable requests for user data
Transparency reports are completely worthless and should be ignored
Technology companies are intentionally deceiving the public about government data requests
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The critics' concern is specifically about SELF-REPORTING without independent audit. This implies that without verification, the reports' accuracy can't be fully trusted — they may be accurate, but we can't know for certain. C is the precisely calibrated inference. A adds 'intentionally deceiving' which is not implied. B is too extreme ('completely worthless'). D is not discussed.

Passage: 'Researchers studying the impact of deforestation in the Amazon found that areas where forest has been replaced by cattle ranching showed not only reduced biodiversity but also lower rainfall levels compared to nearby forested regions. They attributed the rainfall reduction to the loss of the forest's capacity to recycle moisture through transpiration.'

It can most reasonably be inferred that
The rainfall reductions observed are permanent and cannot be reversed even if forest is replanted
Biodiversity loss in the Amazon is caused primarily by reduced rainfall
Cattle ranching is more harmful than all other forms of land use globally
Protecting existing Amazon forest may help maintain regional rainfall patterns
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

If forest → more moisture recycling → more rainfall, then PROTECTING forest would help MAINTAIN rainfall. B follows directly. A is an extreme, unsupported comparison. C over-infers permanence (the passage discusses current effects, not reversibility). D reverses the causal direction (deforestation causes both biodiversity loss AND rainfall reduction — they're both effects, not one causing the other).

Passage: 'The philosopher David Hume argued that the practice of inferring a general principle from a limited number of observations — inductive reasoning — can never be logically justified, since no finite number of confirming instances can rule out a future disconfirming one. He noted, however, that humans rely on induction constantly in practice.'

The passage implies that Hume believed
Inductive reasoning should be completely abandoned in scientific practice
All scientific knowledge derived through induction is false
There is a gap between the logical justification of inductive reasoning and its practical indispensability
Humans are irrational because they rely on unjustified reasoning methods
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

Hume shows: induction is LOGICALLY UNJUSTIFIABLE (can't be proven valid) BUT humans use it CONSTANTLY in practice. This implies a GAP between logical validity and practical use — which is precisely B. A is not implied (Hume notes we use it constantly, not that we should stop). C is too strong. D is too judgmental — Hume describes a philosophical problem, not irrationality.

Passage: 'Historians have documented that the introduction of the automobile in the early twentieth century was initially marketed not as a replacement for the horse but as a cleaner alternative, since horses produced large amounts of manure that created public health problems in cities. Within decades, however, the automobile itself became a major source of urban air pollution.'

The passage most strongly implies that
The automobile was a net improvement over horses in all environmental respects
Technological solutions to environmental problems can themselves generate new environmental problems
The horse was more environmentally friendly than the automobile in all respects
Early automobile manufacturers were aware of but concealed the pollution risks of cars
Medium
Inference
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: cars were adopted as a SOLUTION to a horse pollution problem, but THEN CREATED THEIR OWN pollution problem. This is precisely the pattern of B: technological solutions creating new problems. A is contradicted (cars created air pollution). C is speculative — the passage describes outcomes, not concealment. D is too extreme and not supported.

Passage: 'The novelist Henry James revised his early novels extensively in the last years of his life for a collected edition, producing more elaborate and psychologically complex prose. Many scholars argue that the revisions improved his work, but some readers and critics find the later style overly convoluted compared to the directness of the originals. James himself expressed complete satisfaction with the revisions.'

The passage implies that the value of James's revisions
Cannot be assessed because no original versions survive
Is acknowledged to be inferior to the originals by all readers
Is objectively superior as demonstrated by scholarly consensus
Depends partly on the reader's aesthetic preferences for directness versus psychological complexity
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: scholars argue improvement + some readers prefer originals — a divergence based on aesthetic values (directness vs. complexity). B accurately captures that the assessment depends on reader preferences. A is too strong ('objectively superior' — critical disagreement is noted). C contradicts 'many scholars argue improvement.' D is false (originals survive — they're being compared).

Passage: 'Recent neuroscience research suggests that adolescent brains undergo significant development in the prefrontal cortex — the region associated with impulse control and long-term planning — well into the mid-twenties. These findings have been cited in legal arguments for treating juvenile offenders differently from adults, though critics note that brain development varies significantly among individuals.'

The passage implies that
All individuals under 25 should be treated as juveniles in all legal contexts
The neuroscientific findings support different legal treatment for juveniles but leave open how these findings should be applied to specific cases given individual variation
Adolescent offenders are never responsible for their actions because their brains are underdeveloped
Neuroscience research is unreliable as a basis for legal decisions
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage presents both the legal argument (brain development supports different treatment) AND the caveat (individual variation). Together they imply: the research supports juvenile distinction broadly but individual variation complicates direct application. B captures this nuanced implication. A is too extreme. C says 'never responsible' which is not implied. D is not stated — the passage cites neuroscience as supporting arguments.

Passage: 'The philosopher Peter Singer argues that if it is within our power to prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. He applies this principle to argue that affluent individuals are morally obligated to donate substantial portions of their income to effective charities. Critics argue that his principle, taken seriously, would require a level of sacrifice that is psychologically unsustainable.'

The passage implies that Singer's argument
Has been shown to be logically invalid by its critics
Is primarily relevant to governments rather than individuals
Leads to conclusions that most people would find extremely demanding if consistently applied
Is universally accepted as correct by moral philosophers
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The critics argue Singer's principle would require 'psychologically unsustainable' sacrifice — implying his argument is extremely demanding. B captures this implication accurately. A is contradicted ('critics argue'). C mischaracterizes — critics argue about PRACTICAL DEMANDS, not logical invalidity. D is the opposite of Singer's argument (he specifically addresses individuals).

Passage: 'A historian studying economic records from medieval England found that during periods of plague, surviving workers demanded and received significantly higher wages than before the plague, despite legal attempts by landowners and the crown to keep wages at pre-plague levels. Similar patterns appeared in Continental Europe following major plague outbreaks.'

The passage most strongly suggests that
The medieval plague was economically beneficial for all members of society
Labor shortages caused by high mortality created bargaining power that workers exercised despite legal prohibitions
Medieval rulers were fully supportive of workers' rights to demand higher wages
Wage controls are universally ineffective as economic policy
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

Plague → fewer workers → labor scarcity → workers bargained for higher wages DESPITE legal prohibitions. B captures both the mechanism (labor shortage → bargaining power) and the context (despite prohibitions). A is directly contradicted (rulers tried to keep wages down). C is too broad (being a victim of plague is not an economic benefit). D over-generalizes from this specific historical case.

Passage: 'Critics of growth economics argue that GDP, the primary measure of economic output, fails to capture several dimensions of human welfare. Activities that produce pollution, then require cleanup expenditures, add to GDP twice — once for the pollution and once for the cleanup. Meanwhile, unpaid care work, parenting, and community volunteering — activities with significant social value — add nothing to GDP.'

The passage implies that the author believes
Unpaid care work and volunteering should be financially compensated by governments
The current primary measure of economic output fails to accurately reflect actual human welfare
Pollution and cleanup activities are economically beneficial because they increase GDP
GDP should be immediately abolished and replaced with no alternative
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage presents two specific flaws in GDP: it OVER-counts pollution+cleanup (adds them twice) and UNDER-counts socially valuable unpaid work. This implies GDP is a poor measure of actual welfare. B captures this implication. A is too extreme (no alternative is suggested). C is the absurd conclusion FROM GDP's structure, not the author's view. D is a policy recommendation not stated.

Passage: 'The widespread prescription of ADHD medications to children in the United States has prompted debate. Supporters argue that appropriate medication dramatically improves academic performance and quality of life for genuinely affected children. Critics raise concerns about overdiagnosis, arguing that some children prescribed medication may simply be younger and less mature than their classmates — an effect particularly pronounced among children born just before school enrollment cutoffs.'

The passage most strongly implies that
ADHD medications are ineffective for all children who take them
American schools are intentionally medicating children to improve academic metrics
The diagnosis and medication of ADHD may in some cases reflect relative developmental differences rather than a genuine neurological condition
All children diagnosed with ADHD are misdiagnosed
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The critics' specific concern about YOUNGER children in each class year being more likely to be diagnosed implies that 'ADHD' in some cases reflects RELATIVE IMMATURITY (compared to older classmates) rather than a genuine condition. B captures this precisely. A is too extreme ('all children'). C directly contradicts 'dramatically improves... for genuinely affected children.' D adds conspiratorial intent not in the passage.

Passage: 'Ancient Greek theater originally featured a chorus of performers who commented on the dramatic action, represented public opinion, and addressed the audience directly. Over time, the role of the chorus diminished as playwrights developed individual characters with more complex psychological interiority. By the era of Euripides, the chorus had become largely peripheral to the main dramatic action.'

The passage implies that the development of Greek drama involved
A decline in dramatic quality from the richer choral tradition to the simpler Euripidean style
The deliberate elimination of the chorus by Greek authorities who found it politically dangerous
No meaningful change in dramatic technique over the period described
A shift in focus from collective community perspective toward individual psychological experience
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage describes a movement FROM chorus (collective/public perspective) TO individual characters (psychological interiority). A accurately captures this shift. B adds political motivation not mentioned. C directly contradicts the described development. D is a value judgment not made in the passage (it describes change, not decline in quality).

Passage: 'In markets for credence goods — products whose quality cannot easily be assessed even after purchase, such as medical procedures, legal advice, and car repairs — consumers are particularly vulnerable to being oversupplied with services they do not need. The difficulty of verifying quality shifts power toward the seller, who has both the information advantage and the ability to create demand for their services.'

The passage implies that
Professional licensing and oversight for credence goods providers is economically justified
Consumers in credence goods markets always receive poor quality service
Credence goods markets are more competitive than other types of markets
Consumers should avoid credence goods entirely whenever possible
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows a market failure: information asymmetry gives sellers power to oversupply → consumers are vulnerable. This implies a JUSTIFICATION for external oversight/regulation (licensing, quality verification) to protect consumers. B captures this policy implication. A is too extreme ('always poor quality'). C is the opposite of what the passage implies (less competitive due to information advantage). D is impractical and not stated.

Passage: 'The rapid spread of social media in the 2010s coincided with a notable increase in reported rates of anxiety and depression among adolescents, particularly girls. Researchers debate whether this correlation reflects causation. Some point to experimental studies in which reduced social media use improved wellbeing; others note that adolescents who are already anxious may use social media more as a coping mechanism.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Social media definitively causes depression in adolescent girls
The evidence regarding social media's effects on adolescent mental health remains contested and does not yet support a definitive causal conclusion
Adolescent mental health problems have no cause other than social media use
Reducing social media use is universally beneficial for all adolescents
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage presents: correlation + experimental evidence (some support for causation) + reverse causation alternative. This divided evidence state implies ongoing debate without definitive conclusion. B captures this accurately. A is too strong given the noted debate. C is too broad ('universally beneficial for ALL'). D is extreme and contradicted by the complexity of the research described.

Passage: 'Experimental studies of honesty find that most people — when given the opportunity to cheat on tasks where cheating cannot be detected — cheat, but only a little. They cheat enough to benefit themselves but not so much that they would feel like dishonest people. This pattern holds across many cultures, age groups, and experimental designs.'

The passage implies that
Most people have a threshold beyond which dishonesty conflicts with their self-concept as honest individuals, creating a behavioral constraint on cheating
Human dishonesty is entirely culturally determined
People are fundamentally dishonest when consequences are removed
Cheating behavior varies so widely across individuals that no general pattern can be identified
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The pattern — people cheat A LITTLE but not A LOT even when undetected — implies an internal self-image constraint: people maintain a self-concept as honest, which limits cheating even without external consequences. B captures this psychological implication. A is contradicted (cross-cultural consistency). C is too strong ('fundamentally dishonest'). D is directly contradicted ('holds across many cultures... experimental designs').

Passage: 'The concept of 'learned helplessness,' developed by psychologist Martin Seligman, describes a state in which repeated exposure to uncontrollable adverse events leads an organism to stop attempting to escape or improve its situation, even when escape becomes possible. Seligman initially demonstrated this in laboratory animals and later extended the model to human depression.'

The passage implies that Seligman's research suggested
Depression is caused exclusively by uncontrollable adverse events
Laboratory animal research is generally irrelevant to understanding human psychological conditions
Depression in humans is identical in all respects to the states induced in laboratory animals
Experiences of uncontrollability in a person's history may contribute to the development of depressive states
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: uncontrollable adverse events → learned helplessness → extended to explain human depression. The implication is that EXPERIENCING UNCONTROLLABILITY may contribute to depression in humans. B captures this inference from the model. A is too strong ('identical in all respects'). C is the opposite of what the passage implies (extending animal research to humans). D is too strong ('exclusively caused by').

Passage: 'In the late nineteenth century, the germ theory of disease gradually displaced the miasma theory, which attributed illness to 'bad air' emanating from rotting organic matter. The transition was not immediate: many physicians trained in miasma theory continued practicing according to its principles even as evidence for germ theory accumulated, only retiring or dying as the younger cohort trained in germ theory took over.'

The passage implies that
Germ theory was known to be correct long before miasma theory was practiced
All nineteenth-century physicians were aware of the evidence for germ theory but chose to ignore it
The scientific community immediately and enthusiastically embraces new theories when evidence is compelling
Scientific paradigm shifts may occur partly through generational turnover rather than through the wholesale conversion of existing practitioners
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage explicitly shows that the transition occurred partly because older physicians (trained in miasma theory) were replaced by younger ones (trained in germ theory) — not through universal conversion. B captures this generational mechanism. A is directly contradicted. C is not supported (the passage describes a gradual transition as evidence accumulated). D adds 'chose to ignore' which is not stated.

Passage: 'Environmental economists argue that many costs of industrial production are 'externalized' — borne not by the producing company but by third parties or society at large. Air pollution from a factory, for example, causes health costs to nearby residents that do not appear in the factory's accounting. Without mechanisms to internalize these costs, markets tend to overproduce goods whose production generates negative externalities.'

The passage implies that
Industrial companies are intentionally polluting without regard for human welfare
Market prices for goods with negative externalities are lower than their true social cost
All industrial production should be banned to prevent externalities
Environmental regulations always harm economic efficiency
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

If companies don't pay the full costs (externalized costs aren't in their accounting), their PRODUCTION COSTS are lower than the TRUE SOCIAL COST → they CHARGE LESS than the true cost → MARKET PRICES ARE LOWER than true social cost. B is the precise economic implication. A adds intentionality not stated. C is extreme. D is the opposite of what the passage implies (regulations that internalize costs could IMPROVE efficiency by correcting the market failure).

Passage: 'Research on the 'availability heuristic' shows that people estimate the probability of events based on how easily examples come to mind. Events that receive extensive media coverage — plane crashes, violent crime, terrorism — are typically judged more likely than their statistical frequency warrants, while more common but less dramatic risks — like cardiovascular disease or car accidents — are often underestimated.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Media coverage of dramatic events may distort public risk perception in ways that affect behavior and policy
Plane crashes are more dangerous than car accidents based on the research described
Risk perception is entirely accurate when based on personal experience rather than media
People are incapable of learning the actual statistics about risk
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The availability heuristic + media coverage → overestimation of dramatic but rare events directly implies that media coverage DISTORTS risk perception. B captures this implication about media and policy-relevant risk perception. A is too extreme ('incapable of learning'). C reverses the point (plane crashes are OVERESTIMATED, not actually more dangerous). D is not stated — personal experience is not discussed.

Passage: 'Archaeological evidence suggests that early agricultural societies in the Fertile Crescent experienced nutritional declines compared to the hunter-gatherer societies that preceded them. Skeletal remains show more evidence of vitamin deficiencies, dental caries, and infectious disease in early farming communities. Despite these health costs, agriculture enabled higher population densities and eventually the development of complex civilizations.'

The passage implies that
The development of civilization required the sacrifice of every individual's health outcomes
Agriculture was universally detrimental to human wellbeing
The transition to agriculture involved trade-offs between individual health and collective population growth
Hunter-gatherer societies were healthier in all respects than agricultural societies
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: agriculture → worse individual health BUT → higher population densities and complex civilizations. This is exactly a TRADE-OFF: individual health costs for collective population/civilizational benefits. B captures this precisely. A is too absolute (complex civilizations are described as a benefit). C over-infers beyond what's stated (the passage covers specific nutritional/disease markers, not 'all respects'). D is too extreme ('every individual's health').

Passage: 'In an experiment, researchers showed participants a video of a car accident and then asked them either 'How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?' or 'How fast were the cars going when they hit each other?' Participants who heard the word 'smashed' estimated significantly higher speeds than those who heard 'hit,' and were also more likely to report seeing broken glass — even though there was none in the video.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Participants in the study were deliberately lying about what they saw
Speed estimation from memory is so unreliable it should never be used in legal proceedings
The language used when questioning witnesses may alter their memories of events they actually observed
All eyewitness testimony is fabricated
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The word 'smashed' vs 'hit' changed BOTH speed estimates AND fabricated memories (glass). This directly implies that question wording ALTERS memory construction — B is the precise implication. A is too extreme. C adds 'deliberately lying' when the participants likely genuinely misremembered. D is too strong and a separate policy conclusion.

Passage: 'Globalization has enabled companies to manufacture products in countries with lower labor costs and weaker environmental regulations, a practice known as regulatory arbitrage. This has reduced costs for consumers in wealthy countries while creating employment in developing nations. Critics argue, however, that it also creates a 'race to the bottom' in which countries compete by weakening their own labor and environmental protections to attract investment.'

The passage implies that
The benefits of globalization are unevenly distributed, and the system may create incentives that undermine regulatory protections worldwide
Globalization is entirely harmful to developing nations
Companies that engage in regulatory arbitrage are always acting illegally
All countries should immediately implement identical labor and environmental regulations
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage presents: benefits (lower costs, employment) AND concerns (race to the bottom in regulations). Together they imply uneven distribution of benefits AND systemic risk to regulatory standards. B captures both dimensions. A is contradicted (employment creation is cited as a benefit for developing nations). C adds 'illegally' — regulatory arbitrage is a legal practice. D is a policy recommendation not made in the passage.

Passage: 'Historians of science note that Isaac Newton conducted extensive research into alchemy, biblical chronology, and the occult alongside his work in mathematics and physics. Some historians see this as evidence that Newton was a transitional figure whose worldview combined elements of the emerging scientific method with older mystical traditions, rather than the purely rational scientist of popular imagination.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Popular depictions of historical scientists often flatten the complexity of their actual beliefs and practices
The scientific method did not exist in Newton's time
Newton's work in physics was inspired primarily by his alchemical research
Newton was primarily an alchemist who accidentally discovered physical laws
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows Newton's work was more complex than the 'purely rational scientist' portrayed in popular imagination. This implies popular depictions simplify historical scientists. B is precisely this implication. A reverses the relationship and over-infers causation. C is extreme and directly contradicted. D is not stated — the scientific method was 'emerging' (present, not absent).

Passage: 'Several studies have examined whether financial incentives improve performance. For simple, rule-based tasks with clear right answers, larger incentives generally produce better performance. For complex tasks requiring creativity, problem-solving, or intrinsic motivation, larger financial incentives often produce worse performance than smaller ones.'

The passage implies that
The effect of financial incentives on performance depends critically on the nature of the task
Complex work requires no incentives of any kind to be performed well
Financial incentives should never be used in workplaces
Simple tasks are always more valuable to organizations than complex tasks
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage explicitly shows DIFFERENT effects for different task types — financial incentives help for simple tasks and hurt for complex ones. B is the direct implication. A is too extreme. C over-infers ('no incentives of any kind'). D is a value judgment about organizational priorities not in the passage.

Passage: 'Coral reefs occupy less than 0.1% of the ocean floor but support approximately 25% of all marine species. They are often called the 'rainforests of the sea' not only for their biodiversity but for their structural complexity — the three-dimensional architecture of coral formations creates numerous microhabitats that different species have evolved to exploit over millions of years.'

The passage implies that the destruction of coral reefs would
Only affect species that have no alternative habitat in open ocean environments
Eliminate approximately 0.1% of all marine biodiversity proportionally to their area
Have minimal impact on ocean ecosystems because reefs cover such a small area
Disproportionately threaten marine biodiversity because the species density and ecological complexity of reefs far exceeds their physical extent
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage establishes: reefs = 0.1% of floor but 25% of marine species + millions of years of specialized adaptation. Destroying reefs would DISPROPORTIONATELY threaten biodiversity because their biological importance far exceeds their physical area. B captures this implication. A is directly contradicted by the 0.1% area but 25% species figure. C is the opposite. D is too narrow.

Passage: 'Urbanization rates in sub-Saharan Africa are among the fastest in the world, with millions of people moving to cities annually. However, much of this urbanization occurs in informal settlements lacking basic infrastructure: clean water, sanitation, electricity, and secure land tenure. Economists debate whether this urbanization is producing the productivity gains and quality of life improvements that accompanied urbanization in other regions in earlier centuries.'

The passage implies that
Urban migration in sub-Saharan Africa is driven primarily by government policies rather than individual economic decisions
The absence of infrastructure in African urban settlements may prevent residents from realizing the benefits typically associated with urbanization
Urbanization in sub-Saharan Africa is identical to historical urbanization elsewhere
Informal settlements will inevitably develop the same infrastructure as formal urban areas over time
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows: urbanization is happening BUT without the infrastructure that typically enables productivity gains → economists DEBATE whether the typical benefits are materializing. B is the direct implication. A is contradicted ('debate' implies difference from historical patterns). C adds a cause (government policies) not in the passage. D predicts future development not implied.

Passage: 'When asked to explain their decisions immediately after making them, people typically provide confident, rational-sounding explanations. Research in social psychology and cognitive neuroscience suggests, however, that many decisions are actually made rapidly and intuitively, with the conscious explanation generated afterward to rationalize the choice rather than to describe the process that actually produced it.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Human beings have complete conscious access to the mental processes that produce their decisions
The explanations people give for their decisions may often be post-hoc rationalizations rather than accurate accounts of their decision-making process
Intuitive decision-making is always superior to deliberate, rational decision-making
People are deliberately lying when they explain their decisions
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The research shows decisions are made intuitively, then conscious explanation is GENERATED AFTERWARD to rationalize. This means the explanations aren't accurate accounts — they're post-hoc rationalizations. C captures this precisely. A adds 'deliberately' — the process may be unconscious self-deception. B is the opposite. D adds a value judgment about intuitive superiority not made in the passage.

Passage: 'The 'resource curse' refers to the paradox that countries with abundant natural resources often experience worse economic development, governance, and conflict outcomes than comparable countries without such resources. Researchers attribute this to factors including reduced need to develop productive tax systems, weakened accountability of governments to citizens, and competition among armed groups for control of resource revenues.'

The passage implies that
Countries should refuse to extract their natural resources to avoid the resource curse
Mining and extraction industries are inherently corrupt in all national contexts
Natural resource abundance can undermine the institutional and political conditions that promote long-term economic development
All countries with natural resources will inevitably experience poor governance
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage describes mechanisms: resources → don't need tax systems → weakened accountability + violent competition. These mechanisms UNDERMINE institutions needed for development. B captures this institutional implication. A is too absolute ('inevitably'). C is too strong ('inherently corrupt in all contexts'). D is an extreme policy recommendation not in the passage.

Passage: 'Anthropologists studying forager societies find that they typically work fewer hours to meet subsistence needs than agricultural or industrial workers, and often have more leisure time. This challenges the assumption, common in development economics, that economic intensification represents straightforward progress in human welfare.'

The passage implies that
Forager lifestyles are superior to modern lifestyles in all respects
Economic development measures focused on productivity and GDP may miss important dimensions of human wellbeing such as time autonomy
Anthropological research proves that economic growth reduces human happiness
Modern people should return to forager lifestyles to improve their quality of life
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The finding that foragers work LESS and have MORE leisure challenges the 'economic intensification = progress' assumption — implying development measures (like productivity/GDP) miss dimensions like time autonomy and leisure. B captures this implication. A is too extreme. C is a lifestyle recommendation not made. D over-infers ('proves' is too strong; 'research proves' based on one finding).

Passage: 'In the first decades after the Cuban Revolution, Cuba achieved dramatic improvements in health outcomes — high vaccination rates, reduced infant mortality, expanded medical training — that placed it ahead of many wealthier countries by standard public health metrics. These improvements were achieved despite a relatively low per-capita GDP, challenging the assumption that economic development must precede improvements in public health.'

The passage implies that
Economic development is an irrelevant factor in explaining national health outcomes
Per-capita GDP is not the only determinant of a country's ability to achieve improved public health outcomes
Cuba's health achievements were not genuine or were exaggerated in official statistics
Cuba's political system is superior to other systems in all policy areas
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

The passage shows Cuba achieved good health outcomes WITH LOW GDP — directly challenging the assumption that GDP must precede health improvements. B is the precise implication: GDP is not the ONLY determinant. A is too broad ('all policy areas'). C adds suspicion not in the passage. D is too extreme ('irrelevant factor').

Passage: 'Several city governments have experimented with participatory budgeting, in which residents directly decide how to allocate a portion of the municipal budget through voting and deliberative processes. Evaluations suggest that participatory budgeting tends to shift spending toward infrastructure and services in lower-income neighborhoods that are typically underserved by conventional budget processes.'

The passage most strongly implies that
Conventional budget processes may systematically under-allocate resources to lower-income neighborhoods
Participatory budgeting eliminates all inequities in municipal resource allocation
All cities should immediately implement participatory budgeting for their entire budgets
Participatory budgeting is more expensive to administer than conventional budgeting
Medium
Implication
Inferences & Implications

If participatory budgeting SHIFTS resources toward previously underserved low-income areas, this implies that CONVENTIONAL budgeting was NOT adequately allocating to those areas. B captures this implication. A is too strong ('eliminates all inequities'). C is about administrative cost, not mentioned. D is a policy recommendation not made in the passage.

There is a 33-percentage-point difference between the lowest and highest educational groups.
Exercise rates increase progressively with each higher level of educational attainment, from 18% among those without a high school diploma to 51% among graduate degree holders.
Adults with graduate degrees report the highest exercise rates at 51%.

Data & Charts
Quantitative Data & Charts

The argument is about a PROGRESSIVE ASSOCIATION between education and exercise across ALL groups. Passage: The deep-sea anglerfish produces its own light through bacteria housed in a specialized organ. Remarkably, juveniles are not born with these bacteria; they must acquire them from the surrounding seawater within days of hatching.

An anglerfish's ability to produce light depends on an environmental factor, not solely on inheritance.

Hard
Inference
Inferences & Implications
